chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Count Basie from Moten's band to the Grand Terrace; Horace's riffs for Basie
summary: Fletcher recommended Basie to Ed Fox for the Grand Terrace; Horace made a few riff-based originals for Basie, who invited him to send charts. A tangent on Redbank, New Jersey musicians follows.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Uh-huh. What sorts of things did you do for Count Basie?
Well, Count's quite a guy, you know.
There's an easy going guy.

Yes, he is. He's another guy that -- he came up in those days with Fletcher. In fact, before I tell you about the writing part, Count was in Kansas City, you know, and used to be in the band out of Kansas City called Benny Moten. And his brother, Buster Moten, used to direct that band, and he played squeeze box, accordion.
It's Moten, isn't it -- I think.
Yeah. Yeah, and And Count Basie was playing piano, Moten, (unintelligible).
that was a swinging band then.
Yeah, it's well known. There are a lot of good people that came out of that band.
Oh, a lot of great Musicians that -- Big Joe Page, the bass, --
Right. Pres Young was --

Oh, Pres was in that band. That was a great band. And when Count took it over. He wanted to come to Chicago, and Fletcher was instrumental in getting Count in the Grand Terrace. Buck Clayton, the trumpet player, was in that band --Harry and Sweets Edison. Oh, man, those are legends, those guys. And when Fletcher went out on the road, Ed Fox's Grand Terrace was the popular club in Chicago, and Fletcher recommended Basie to this gentleman that owned the club, and went in there and did a terrific Basie was a man that could do the job. And he went right on, man, If course, it was the ambition of every musician and bandleader to get to New York during in those days, you know. If it wasn't for recording purposes, it was for some other reason, because it was popular. And that was that.

And I made a couple of original things for Basie, and I don't know if he recorded them or not, but I'd heard that band, and it was easy to write, you know, and he often told me, he says, 'If you have anything good that you think is good, and you know my style, he said, send it on in to the office. The old man will take care of you.' You know, one of those
things. And I used to take some riffs, fix them up, because he was primarily interested in things like that.
Yeah, that was those that hold a whole Kansas City blues band tradition. Walter Page and Benny Moten.
Those stocks that Joe Stutte came out in those days.
Oh, man, and -- let's see. You know he was living in RedBank, New Jersey, for a long time.
"The Kid from RedBank."
He was from RedBank. Yeah, that's a tune by that was two by their name. And who's that great drummer that was with him from RedBank? Wasn't it Joe Jones?
Yeah, I think so.
I think That was the original drummer that he had.
I believe so. I'd have to check it out, but --
That, or either I'm thinking of Sonny Greer. I think Sonny Greer was from Redbank, New Jersey.
Sonny Greer was with Ellington for a long time.
Yes. But I think he was from Redbank, New Jersey, too, I think.
Was he? Yeah.
I know that they had two guys there. One was the piano player, and the other one was the drummer.
They were from Redbank, New Jersey. But Basie made a lot of great things.
